0: Zero as a number in its own right, with rules for adding and multiplying by it, was set out by the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta in 628 CE. The Romans had no numeral for it.
1: One is neither prime nor composite. It divides every whole number, and every number multiplied by 1 stays the same.
2: The only even prime. Every other even number is divisible by 2, so it is composite.
3: The first odd prime. In Cantonese, 3 sounds like the word for life, while in Mandarin it can also suggest 'scatter'.
4: The most avoided number in East Asia: in Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese and Korean it sounds like 'death', and many buildings skip the 4th floor.
7: Widely seen as lucky in Western culture, and Japan honours its Seven Lucky Gods. It is also the smallest number that needs four squares to write as a sum of squares (4 + 1 + 1 + 1).
8: China's luckiest digit: 八 (bā) sounds like 发 (fā), 'to prosper'. The Beijing Olympics opened on 8 August 2008 at 8 pm local time.
9: Nine splits cultures. It is lucky in China (it sounds like 'long-lasting') and Thailand (it sounds like 'step forward'), but avoided in Japan, where ku sounds like 'suffering'.
12: Twelve months, twelve signs of the Western zodiac and twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac. The dozen sits behind many old units of measure.
13: Feared in Western superstition (triskaidekaphobia): many hotels and towers skip a 13th floor. In Italy, 13 is often considered lucky.
17: Italy's unlucky number: XVII can be rearranged as VIXI, Latin for 'I have lived', which implies death.
18: In Judaism the letters of chai ('life') add up to 18, so gifts and donations are often given in multiples of 18.
24: Hours in a day, and the number of solar terms in the traditional Chinese calendar.
39: Afghanistan's stigmatised number: news reports since 2011 describe drivers refusing number plates with 39 and owners avoiding phone numbers that contain it. In Japan the same digits read san-kyū, 'thank you'. Read why.
42: In Douglas Adams's The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (1979), 42 is the answer a supercomputer gives to the ultimate question.
60: The base of Babylonian mathematics, which is why we still count 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour.
64: A chessboard has 64 squares, and 64 is both a square (8²) and a cube (4³).
88: Double 8 means double prosperity in Chinese culture, and 88 is chat slang for 'bye-bye'. A standard piano has 88 keys.
99: Doubled 9 (久久) suggests 'forever' in Chinese. In Islam, 99 names of God are traditionally recited.
100: The base of the percentage, and of most currency subunits: 100 cents, 100 paise.
101: A favourite Indian gift amount, because one more than a round sum signals a fresh start. In US colleges, '101' marks an introductory course.
108: Sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism: prayer malas carry 108 beads, and Japanese temple bells ring 108 times on New Year's Eve. India's emergency ambulance line uses the same number.
168: In Chinese, 1-6-8 sounds like 一路发, 'prosper all the way', which makes it a favourite in phone numbers and shop addresses.
250: In Chinese slang, 二百五 (250) calls someone a fool, so it is a number to avoid in gifts and prices.
314: The first digits of π (3.14). Pi Day falls on 14 March, written 3/14 in the United States.
360: Degrees in a full turn, a convention that traces back to Babylonian base-60 astronomy.
365: Days in a common year; a leap year adds a 366th day.
404: The web's best-known error code: HTTP 404 Not Found.
439: The heart of this site's own number. 439 is the 85th prime and the sum of three consecutive primes (139 + 149 + 151). London's orchestras tuned to A = 439 Hz from 1896, the Vandals took Carthage in AD 439, and in India 'Section 439' long meant bail before a High Court or Sessions Court. Read the full 439439 story.
440: Concert pitch: A = 440 Hz was agreed at a London conference in 1939 and later became the international standard ISO 16.
495: Kaprekar's constant for 3-digit numbers: arrange any 3-digit number's digits (not all the same) from high to low, subtract the low-to-high version, repeat, and you always reach 495.
501: A classic Indian gift amount: adding one rupee to a round sum signals a new beginning.
518: In Chinese, 5-1-8 sounds like 我要发, 'I will prosper', a coveted ending for phone numbers.
520: 520 (wǔ èr líng) sounds like 我爱你, 'I love you', in Mandarin, so 20 May has become an unofficial Valentine's Day in China.
666: The 'number of the beast' in the Book of Revelation (13:18). In Chinese internet slang the same digits mean 'awesome, smooth'.
786: Many South Asian Muslims write 786, the abjad numerical value of the Bismillah, at the top of letters and documents.
888: Triple prosperity in Chinese culture. Phone numbers and number plates full of 8s command large premiums.
911: The emergency number in the United States and Canada. The first 911 call in the US was made in Haleyville, Alabama, in 1968.
999: The UK's emergency number since 1937, the world's oldest emergency telephone number.
1000: A thousand, the basis of the metric prefix kilo-. Above this, Indian English groups digits in lakhs and crores.
1001: 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13, which is why every ABCABC number divides by all three. In India ₹1,001 is a classic gift amount, and The Thousand and One Nights gave the number literary fame. See the trick.
1234: The simplest counting run, and the classic example of a PIN that is easy to guess.
1314: 一生一世, 'a whole lifetime': a favourite in Chinese gift amounts and wedding dates.
1729: The Hardy–Ramanujan number: the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways (1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³).
1947: The year of independence for India (15 August 1947) and Pakistan (14 August 1947).
6174: Kaprekar's constant: take any 4-digit number with at least two different digits, subtract its ascending arrangement from its descending one, repeat, and you reach 6174 within seven steps.
65536: 2¹⁶, the number of values that fit in 16 bits, a familiar limit in computing (0 to 65,535).
100000: One lakh in the Indian numbering system, written 1,00,000.
142857: The cyclic number: multiply it by 1 through 6 and the same digits come back rotated (142857 × 2 = 285714). It is the repeating block of 1/7.
439439: This site's own number: 439 written twice, so it equals 439 × 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 × 439. On a phone keypad it spells HEYHEY. Read the full story.
1000000: One million, or ten lakh in the Indian system.
5201314: Chinese number slang combining 520 ('I love you') and 1314 ('a whole lifetime'): 'I love you forever'.
